faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Kingstree attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Kingstree home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

Hemingway.wildlife_intro:
Hemingway keeps our crew busy around the farm and Black Mingo Creek country in the county's east. Two problems account for most visits: gray squirrels in town canopy streets, and skunks denning at outbuildings.

Early-1900s farm-town housing, tobacco-era homes, and postwar ranches sit on crawlspaces above soil that stays damp much of the year. Flat, wet ground after summer storms pushes snakes and burrowing animals onto higher, drier lots — frequently the lots with houses on them — which is when many of our calls here start.

Removal without repair does not hold in Hemingway, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: Pigeons and starlings are nesting in my Greeleyville vents. Can they be removed?
faqs.a: Pigeons, European starlings, and house sparrows are the birds we can work on in Greeleyville — vents screened, nests cleared, and spikes or netting fitted so the birds move on. Native birds are different: woodpeckers, chimney swifts, and nesting songbirds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so those jobs are deterrence and timing, waiting out the nest and sealing after the young fledge. Around Black River farm roads in the county's west, vent and soffit nests are the calls we see most.

faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Greeleyville that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Greeleyville.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Greeleyville and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the Black River farm roads in the county's west. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in sandy field-edge yards, then about bats in tobacco-barn and gable roosts.

Housing here runs from historic in-town streets to farm roads, and most of it predates modern sealed construction — open vents and pier foundations are the norm. Blackwater rivers and swamp drains thread this farm country, and wildlife follows them: raccoons, opossums, and armadillos work the wet edges, then den in the nearest barn, porch, or crawlspace.

Before we leave a Greeleyville home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Lane attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Stuckey lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Stuckey home. Should I be worried?

We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went.
